heading: Reading your place
body: The permaculture course for small farmers of South Africa.
Read the land before you change it. Find where the water goes, where the sun sets/crosses, where the wind goes, and where the cold air stays.
These things you see will lead you in choosing plants, trees, buildings, paths and water. They are the beginning of good design.

heading: Why this is important
body: Every farm already has working arrangements before we add anything.
Rain already follows lines over the ground. The sun already warms some places more than others. The wind already finds gaps and ridges. Cold air already stays in low places.
When you read these ways first, you put water, plants, trees and buildings where they can work together with the land.

heading: Learning outcomes
body: At the end of this topic you will be able to follow water over your land and find where it comes out/leaves.
You will learn the position of the sun, shade, wind, frost and slopes.
You will use an A-frame level to follow contour lines.
You will draw a simple map of the place that can show water flow, seasonal winds, frost areas, existing plants, zones and sectors.

heading: Lesson 1: Where the rain goes
body: Before you collect water, learn where it is already going.

Look from a safe place during heavy rain. When it is safe afterwards, walk on your land. Look for small streams of water (rills), places where water spreads, ponds, and where water goes out of your property.
Some excess water needs a safe way to go away so that it does not cause damage.

heading: Look: water slows, enters the ground, and comes out
body: The picture shows rain coming down a hill. Follow where it speeds up, where it spreads, where it enters the ground, where it gathers, and then where it comes out of the ground/leaves.

heading: Follow contour lines with an A-frame
body: Build an A-frame level with three poles and a string tied to a heavy object.
Move it over the ground to find points at one level of height. Join these points to follow the contour line.

The A-frame can help you mark points at one level of height and follow a contour line. Its marks are for observation only, not design or permission for earth-digging work. Before digging, ask for the site to be assessed. Soil, slope, water outflow, water movement in heavy rain and a safe route for excess water are all important. Ask a trained local advisor.

heading: See the water before building
body: Water speeds up and gets the power to wash away as it goes down the slope.
There is no single placement rule followed on all slopes. Look where water goes and where it gathers.
Contours placed badly can increase soil erosion, and soil that absorbs water slowly can hold too much water. Choose whatever water works suit your place and plan a safe route for excess water.

heading: Lesson 2: Learn sun and shade
body: In many places in South Africa, especially in winter, the sun is in the north. Its path changes with the season and with where you are.
North-facing slopes usually get a lot of sun and can get hot and become drier. South-facing slopes are usually cool and more moist. Frost can gather in low places where cold air stays.
Look at your own place before choosing where to put tender plants, trees or buildings.

heading: Look: follow the sun across the whole place
body: Follow the sun, a building, a tree and their shadows over the slope. Compare the high summer sun and the low winter sun.

heading: Look at winter shadows before building
body: The winter sun is low and further north than the summer sun.
A wall or shade cloth can give a bed shade for a longer time in winter than in summer. Look at the real shadows before you build or fix a shade structure in the place.
Stand in that place at 8am, noon, 4pm on a winter day. Look where the shadow falls.

heading: Protect plants that feel the frost
body: Pawpaw and young citrus trees feel the frost (are frost-sensitive).
Keep tender plants away from known low places where frost gathers. Check local frost before planting.

heading: Lesson 3: Learn wind, frost and slopes
body: Wind can damage plants on a small farm.

The direction and strength of damaging wind changes by region, by season, and with the gaps and ridges of your place. Walk your land on windy days. Record where the damaging wind comes from and what it affects. Check local weather records before putting up a windbreak.
Wind, cold air and slopes are all important when choosing places for plants and shelters.

heading: Look: see wind and cold air on the map
body: A place protected from wind may still collect cold air. Look at wind protection and frost risk separately.

heading: Cold air goes down the slope
body: On clear, still nights, cold air can move down the slope and gather in low places. These places can be colder than the surrounding slopes.
Frost is ice that forms on a cold surface. Fog alone does not show that ice has formed, and frost damage can happen without visible ice.

Look for ice and plant damage, compare low ground and slopes, and look at the lowest temperature where you can. Mark places where cold or damage stays a long time. Keep delicate plants away from the cold places you have seen.
Compare the places you can choose for growing seedlings in the local frost season. Check local records of lowest temperatures or ask a local agricultural advisor before choosing a permanent place.

heading: Choose moving air and temperature
body: Put the nursery for frost-sensitive seedlings outside the cold places you have seen. Compare the places you can choose in the local frost season. Check local records of lowest temperatures or ask a local agricultural advisor before choosing a permanent place. Also look at the sun and damaging wind. No hill place guarantees the absence of frost.

For tomatoes with the late blight problem, good air movement and morning sun can help leaves dry. Cold, humid weather for a long time may encourage this disease. Moving the bed alone does not control late blight. Also seek local plant-health advice.

heading: Lesson 4: Start the map of your place
body: A site map needs paper, a measuring tape, a compass, and time to walk on your land.
Walk along the boundary and make a first drawing. Write it 'not measured to scale' until you check its distances. Mark north. Add house, trees, water, paths and fences.
After that, draw the paths you have seen. Your map becomes the framework of the design of the whole small farm.

heading: Look: draw the land you have now
body: Use the picture as a guide: boundary, buildings, paths, water, slopes and direction arrows. Draw what is already there before planning change.

heading: Let plants help you read the land
body: Look where frost stays a long time and where the ground smells of moisture in the dry months.
Notice the existing plants. Mark where khakibos or blackjack grows densely.
These plants can grow in disturbed places, but their presence alone does not show whether the soil is compacted/dense. Test the soil before deciding what that place means for your design.

heading: Add seasons, zones and sectors
body: Mark summer wind and winter wind separately. They may come from different directions, so a windbreak or plant position that works in one season may be unsuitable in another.
Put your zones and sectors on the same base map.
Update the drawing every season of the year. A pencil map that you actually use is really more important than a perfect map drawn once.

heading: Field work
body: When it is safe after heavy rain, walk on your land. Mark small streams of water, spreading water, ponds, and where water leaves your property. Notice where excess water might need a safe way to go away.
Come back very early in the morning on a cold June morning. Mark fog, frozen drops of fog, and places where frost stays a long time.
On paper, draw your boundary, mark north, then add house, water, paths, fences, slopes and existing plants.

heading: Field action
body: Build an A-frame level with three poles and a string tied to a heavy object.

Use it to mark points at one level of height and follow the contour line. This is observation, not design of earth-digging works. Before digging, ask a trained local advisor to assess the site and plan a safe route for excess water.
Add arrows for summer and winter wind, shade observations at 8am, noon and 4pm, and your zones and sectors. Keep the map and update it.
